reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents with the rapid onset of symmetrical limb swelling and induration, often following unaccustomed strenuous exercise
The skin develops a woody, peau d'orange appearance with the characteristic 'groove sign' where veins appear depressed along indurated fascia
In contrast to systemic sclerosis, the fingers, face, and internal organs are typically spared and Raynaud phenomenon and nailfold changes are absent
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common early but may be transient and is not required for diagnosis
Full-thickness biopsy including fascia shows thickened, inflamed fascia with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils
MRI demonstrates fascial thickening and enhancement and helps guide biopsy site and monitor response
Most patients respond well to systemic corticosteroids, sometimes with a steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate
An association with haematological disorders means a search for underlying malignancy is prudent in atypical or refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic fasciitis is an uncommon fibrosing disorder characterised by inflammation and thickening of the deep fascia. The trigger is unknown but strenuous physical exertion frequently precedes onset. An immune-mediated process recruits eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells into the fascia, with release of profibrotic mediators driving collagen deposition and fascial fibrosis. The resulting induration tethers overlying skin and can cause joint contractures. Peripheral eosinophilia and hypergammaglobulinaemia reflect the underlying inflammatory activation, and an association with clonal haematological disease is recognised.
additionalDifferentials: Morphoea (localised scleroderma), especially deep or generalised variants
additionalInvestigations: Full-thickness incisional biopsy extending to fascia and muscle to confirm fascial inflammation and fibrosis
Full blood count with differential to detect peripheral eosinophilia
MRI of affected limbs showing fascial thickening and contrast enhancement
Serum immunoglobulins and inflammatory markers (often raised gammaglobulins, ESR, aldolase)
Autoantibody panel to help exclude systemic sclerosis and overlap conditions
Screening for associated haematological disorders in atypical or resistant disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive contractures threatening limb function
Cytopenias or other features suggesting an associated haematological malignancy
Poor response to corticosteroids raising concern for an alternative fibrosing disorder
Aplastic anaemia or myeloproliferative features in association with the fasciitis
reference.prognosis: Many patients achieve substantial improvement or remission with prompt corticosteroid therapy, though residual induration or contractures may persist, and relapse can occur on tapering. An associated haematological disorder worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing the sparing of digits and absence of Raynaud phenomenon
Taking too superficial a biopsy that fails to sample the fascia and yields a non-diagnostic result
Assuming a normal eosinophil count excludes the diagnosis when eosinophilia is transient
Delaying treatment and allowing fixed contractures to develop
Failing to screen for an underlying haematological disorder in refractory cases
management: Prompt high-dose systemic corticosteroids to control fascial inflammation, followed by a gradual taper
Early steroid-sparing immunosuppression, usually methotrexate, especially with morphoea-like skin change or incomplete corticosteroid response
Physiotherapy and stretching to prevent and treat joint contractures and preserve function
Additional agents such as mycophenolate, ciclosporin, tocilizumab, intravenous immunoglobulin or rituximab for refractory disease
Monitor response clinically and with MRI, tracking peripheral eosinophilia and inflammatory markers
Screen for and manage an associated clonal haematological disorder
Rheumatology referral with occupational therapy input for hand function
